title: A liver lesion on a scan

guidelineVersions: European Association for the Study of the Liver, Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of benign liver tumours, Journal of Hepatology 2016;65:386–398
NICE NG50, Cirrhosis in over 16s, 2016, recommendations 1.2.4–1.2.5

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in an HPB MDT-style applied-knowledge station. The examiner provides this written report: “63-year-old, previous colorectal adenocarcinoma treated three years ago; ultrasound shows a 2.8 cm heterogeneous indeterminate right-lobe liver lesion.”
brief.task: Explain the differential, further characterisation, safe referral and patient communication.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Interpret the lesion through risk factors and a definitive imaging pathway, not morphology alone.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling an indeterminate lesion definitely metastatic or ordering immediate biopsy without MDT review.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Ask for previous cancer, liver disease and scan history.

flow: Avoid premature biopsy and involve HPB MDT

grid.label: Risk context
grid.fail: Ignores cancer history and chronic liver disease.
grid.borderline: Asks about cancer but not cirrhosis.
grid.pass: Identifies colorectal cancer history and compares cirrhosis risk.
grid.high: Integrates history and imaging pretest probability.

grid.label: Report interpretation
grid.fail: Calls lesion diagnostic on ultrasound alone.
grid.pass: States enhancement and washout require multiphase characterisation.
grid.high: Compares metastasis, haemangioma and HCC profiles without overclaiming.

grid.label: Benign haemangioma
grid.fail: Believes all liver lesions require biopsy.
grid.borderline: Recognises haemangioma but no imaging features.
grid.pass: Describes typical peripheral nodular enhancement and delayed centripetal fill-in.
grid.high: Explains why the pattern changes management in an otherwise healthy liver.

grid.label: Malignant differential
grid.fail: Rules out metastasis in cancer survivor.
grid.pass: Considers colorectal metastasis and HCC in at-risk liver.
grid.high: States imaging appearance and background disease determine next investigation.

grid.label: Appropriate imaging
grid.pass: Recommends contrast MRI or liver-protocol multiphase imaging.
grid.high: Chooses imaging according to cancer suspicion and previous scans.

grid.label: Biopsy safety
grid.pass: Avoids unplanned biopsy pending HPB MDT assessment.
grid.high: Explains bleeding and seeding/diagnostic planning concerns without absolute contraindication.

grid.label: MDT and pathway
grid.pass: Refers suspicious lesion for HPB/liver MDT review.
grid.high: Coordinates staging and tissue decisions through appropriate specialist team.

grid.label: HCC surveillance
grid.borderline: Knows cirrhosis matters but not frequency.
grid.pass: Mentions six-month ultrasound surveillance in relevant cirrhosis.
grid.high: Separates surveillance from investigation of a detected suspicious lesion.

grid.label: Communication
grid.pass: Explains differential, targeted imaging and follow-up.
grid.high: Addresses anxiety and provides a specific safety and results plan.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would not ask about alcohol, hepatitis or cirrhosis, or about when and how the bowel cancer was treated; the scan answers that.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What do you make of the ultrasound finding?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Any liver lesion after cancer means metastasis.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, so I do not need to think about benign tumours or underlying liver disease.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will ask for biopsy today without reviewing the old scans.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is unnecessary once an ultrasound shows a lesion.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Possibly, but all liver lesions need a biopsy to be sure, so I would biopsy it either way.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What would you tell the patient?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Your cancer has definitely come back. You do not need any specialist review.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What if the patient also has cirrhosis?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It makes no difference to the differential or liver follow-up.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A 63-year-old with previous colorectal cancer has an incidental 2.8-cm liver lesion. What additional history matters?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would review cancer stage and surveillance scans, previous liver lesions, weight loss and symptoms, and chronic liver disease or viral hepatitis.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ultrasound calls it heterogeneous, but not diagnostic. Your interpretation?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It is indeterminate; ultrasound alone cannot establish whether this is benign or malignant in a patient with cancer history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Colorectal liver metastasis, haemangioma and, especially with cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Contrast-enhanced liver MRI or appropriate multiphase liver-protocol imaging, taking account of previous cancer scans.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Peripheral nodular arterial enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in on delayed phases.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you decide whether to biopsy?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would not arrange an unplanned biopsy. Imaging and the HPB MDT should establish whether tissue is needed and the safest route.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: HPB and relevant oncology teams, with radiology review and staging if malignancy is suspected.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How is HCC surveillance performed in relevant cirrhosis?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: NICE NG50 recommends six-monthly ultrasound with or without AFP for specified patients with cirrhosis; that does not replace proper work-up of a new lesion.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The patient asks, “Is it definitely cancer?”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No, not from this report. We need a better-characterising scan and specialist review, and I would explain when and how the result will be communicated.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Start with the risk profile rather than the label on the scan.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would obtain the colorectal primary pathology and stage, treatment and CEA trend, compare past CTs, and ask about hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcohol-related disease and metabolic risk. These factors materially alter the probability of metastasis or HCC.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The ultrasound report says 2.8 cm, heterogeneous, vascular and indeterminate.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That is descriptive, not a diagnosis. A single-phase description does not establish a classic enhancement pattern, so I would not label it metastasis or haemangioma without dedicated imaging.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Which differential possibilities would you prioritise?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Given previous colorectal cancer, metastatic disease is a leading concern; a typical benign haemangioma remains possible. HCC rises in probability with cirrhosis or viral hepatitis.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Explain what would support a haemangioma.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Discontinuous peripheral nodular enhancement followed by progressive inward fill-in on delayed contrast images is characteristic. A confidently typical lesion in a suitable context usually needs no intervention.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What imaging pathway is most useful now?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Review existing cancer staging scans first, then request dedicated contrast-enhanced liver MRI or a multiphase CT protocol as appropriate, with specialist radiology interpretation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The referring team suggests image-guided biopsy tomorrow.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would defer an unplanned biopsy until the HPB MDT reviews imaging; many benign lesions are diagnosed non-invasively, and tissue strategy should account for risks and future oncological management.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What next if metastasis remains likely?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: HPB and colorectal oncology MDT discussion, evaluation of extrahepatic disease, liver disease reserve and treatment options. A finding should not be called resectable from a short ultrasound report.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How does HCC surveillance fit into this case?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Six-month ultrasound ± AFP is surveillance for appropriate cirrhotic patients under NICE NG50. Once a lesion is found, it requires diagnostic characterisation, not another six-month surveillance wait.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The patient is frightened this means recurrent cancer.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would acknowledge the concern, state that it is a possibility rather than a confirmed diagnosis, arrange a definite scan and MDT review, and identify who will relay results and when.

failures.move: Orders biopsy without imaging or MDT review
Discharges a potentially malignant indeterminate liver lesion with no specialist pathway.
Informs the patient that metastasis is proven by an indeterminate ultrasound

recovery.when: If you called this metastatic on ultrasound alone
recovery.line: I should not have called this metastatic on ultrasound alone; I need dedicated contrast imaging and HPB radiology review.

recovery.when: Before deciding whether tissue is required
recovery.line: Let me review the previous cancer stage and old scans before deciding whether tissue is required.

knowledge.fact: Cancer history and background liver disease inform malignancy probability and imaging choice.
Typical haemangioma contrast enhancement is peripheral globular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in.
Contrast MRI is preferred when a benign lesion is suspected; CT may be preferable when malignancy suspected.
When imaging is uncertain, biopsy decisions should be considered by an experienced MDT.
In suitable cirrhosis, NICE recommends ultrasound with or without AFP every six months for HCC surveillance.
A new indeterminate lesion requires diagnostic investigation rather than routine surveillance alone.

recall.think: Characterise the liver risk background and cancer history.
recall.say: Explain the lesion is indeterminate rather than confirmed malignant.
do: Review old scans; arrange contrast liver imaging and HPB MDT.

numbers.meaning: HCC surveillance interval is 6 months in eligible cirrhosis

recall.trap: Do not biopsy or label metastasis solely from ultrasound.
